people.label: Harry M. Reid
people.narrative: Reid is the appropriator who created the funded lineage and then tried to seal it. As Majority Leader he worked with Appropriations chairman Daniel Inouye and Ted Stevens in 2007 to direct roughly $22 million into the defense black budget for what became AAWSAP at DIA — AARO's own 2024 report states flatly that 'at the direction of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV), the Defense Appropriations Acts of Fiscal Years 2008 and 2010 appropriated $22 million for the DIA.' Reid took repeated DIA briefings on contract status: talking papers survive from January 2009, May 2009 and November 2009. On 24 June 2009 he wrote to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requesting that portions of what he called the 'Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program' be placed in a Restricted Special Access Program with a bigoted access list, protecting methodologies for identifying and engineering advanced technologies, personnel and oversight details, and the involvement of private contractors and industry partners. That letter is the most important single document in this domain because it establishes that the Senate Majority Leader believed the program was producing something warranting SAP protection with a compartmented access list. DoD refused. Reid later said publicly that $22 million was not enough and that failing to study the subject would be malpractice, and called the program one of the good things he did in his congressional service. He died 28 December 2021.
people.tierRationale: His authorship of the appropriation is confirmed in an official DoD report and his SAP request survives as a signed primary document with a DoD response chain.

people.label: Daniel K. Inouye
people.sub: US Senator (D-HI); Chairman, Senate Appropriations Committee
people.narrative: Inouye is the reason the money moved without a floor fight. As chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee (and previously chair of Defense Appropriations) he controlled the vehicle through which discretionary defense spending is written, and his agreement let Reid and Ted Stevens route roughly $22 million into the classified annex of the FY2008 defense appropriation rather than into a line item anyone would have to defend publicly. The mechanism matters more than the man: an appropriation placed in the black budget by three senators, two of them the ranking figures of the appropriations process, is not subject to the authorizing committees' scrutiny and does not appear in any public budget justification. That is the precise structural gap the modern disclosure fight is about. Inouye had a decades-long record of pushing back on intelligence-community secrecy from inside the process — he co-chaired the Iran-Contra committee — which makes his participation here a deliberate act rather than a favour. He died in office on 17 December 2012, the same year AAWSAP/AATIP was terminated.
people.tierRationale: His role is documented in reporting and is structurally necessary to the appropriation, but no primary document naming him on the AAWSAP earmark has been released.

entities.desc: The funding instrument, and the reason the whole thing stayed invisible. aawsap.desc: Document custody map for AAWSAP. The releasable record falls into six groups. (1) Procurement: solicitation HHM402-08-R-0211 with its statement of work (SOW_Aerospace.pdf, 22 Aug 2008), the award document HHM402-08-C-0072 released as FOIA-00349-2018 (13 Oct 2022), the commercial-items order released as FOIA-00269-2018 (28 Jun 2023), and the FY10 option modification (2 Sep 2009). (2) Status briefings: DI_Brief_2008 (16 Dec 2008), DI_Brief_2009 (8 May 2009), Contract_Status_24Aug09, and an undated Contract_Status_Briefing. (3) The Reid file: three DIA talking papers (5 Jan 2009, 4 May 2009, 19 Nov 2009), the Reid briefing deck of 8 May 2009, and Reid's SAP request of 24 Jun 2009. (4) The SAP decision chain: deliverables review U-429-09-DWO-IM (30 Oct 2009), OUSDI_IM_on_AATIP_Final, DIA memo U-09-2660CE-IM (13 Nov 2009), and the 18-page packet presented to the Deputy Secretary of Defense (17 Nov 2009). (5) The transition file: DIA info memo U-10-2552CE-IM-ATL to USD(AT&L), released in draft and in a four-page final under FOIA-00255-2022. (6) The deliverables: 37 of 38 DIRDs, released individually and as a bulk archive, plus the 9 Jan 2018 DIA letter to the Senate Armed Services Committee that lists all 38 by title and author. What is NOT in the record: the BAASS Ten Month Report (leaked, never officially released), the Utah ranch investigation report (DIA reports no records), the 19 Jun 2007 Lacatski-to-Bigelow letter (DIA reports no records), the SECRET/NOFORN version of DIRD 37, obligation-by-year funding data, the AAWSAP personnel roster, and whatever comprises the 100-plus reports Lacatski describes.

aatip.desc: The naming question, stated precisely, because it is the single most-abused fact in this domain. Four designations appear in primary documents: (1) Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP) — the contract title, used in the solicitation, the award, and all DIA contracting paperwork 2008-2010. (2) Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program (AAITP) — Harry Reid's usage in his 24 June 2009 letter to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. (3) Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP) — described in the November 2009 DoD packet as the 'unclassified nickname', and the name DIA used exclusively in its December 2010 transfer memo and its January 2018 letter to Congress. (4) 'AAWSAP/AATIP' — the compound AARO adopted in 2024 to treat them as one thing. DoD's public position since June 2019 depends on treating AAWSAP and AATIP as distinguishable enough that a person can have had a role in one and no 'assigned responsibilities' for the other. The November 2009 packet, which lists all three names for the same effort on the same page, is the document that makes that position difficult to sustain.

gaps: The BAASS Ten Month Report (494 pp, July 2009) has never been officially released. Only a leaked copy circulates. FOIA it directly from DIA by title and date; if DIA claims no records, appeal and demand a search of the Defense Warning Office contract deliverable file, which the contract's monthly-reporting clause proves must exist.

The 'Utah Ranch Investigation: August 2009-February 2010' report described by Lacatski, Kelleher and Knapp: DIA reports no records located. This is the single most important negative FOIA result in the domain and has not been litigated. A FOIA suit forcing an adequacy-of-search declaration would be high value.

Obligation-by-year funding data for contract HHM402-08-C-0072. The $10M base is documented; the remaining ~$12M of the $22M appropriation has no released obligation record, and DIA procurement is exempt from FPDS/USAspending reporting under 10 USC 424. Try DIA's contracting activity directly, and try the DoD Comptroller for the FY2008/FY2010 classified annex line.

The exact appropriations bill language and account line into which the $22M was placed has never been released. Senate Appropriations Committee classified annex records for FY2008 and FY2010 are the target.

The SECRET/NOFORN version of the high-energy laser weapons DIRD (transmittal item 37) remains withheld. It is the only one of the 38 not released and a mandatory declassification review request is the obvious next step.

No AATIP charter, tasking order, delegation of authority or organisation chart covering the 2011-2017 period has ever been produced by OUSD(I). DoD's denial of Elizondo's role rests entirely on press guidance. This is the highest-value single document gap in the domain.

The AAWSAP/BAASS personnel roster. Neither DIA nor the contractor has released a staff list, so the number of people who held program access, and who they were, is unknown. Jay Stratton's exact AAWSAP role is unconfirmed.
The 19 June 2007 Lacatski letter to Robert Bigelow: DIA reports no records. Bigelow presumably holds the recipient copy. No one appears to have asked him for it on the record.

Lacatski's claim of 'more than 100 thick, highly detailed reports' of UFO case data is unverified and unindexed. If it is accurate, there is a body of AAWSAP deliverables an order of magnitude larger than the 38 DIRDs whose custody is entirely unaccounted for.

The BAASS case database (the secure server infrastructure described in the Ten Month Report) — its disposition after 2012 is unknown. Whether it was transferred to the government, retained by BAASS, or destroyed is undocumented, and it would contain the MUFON Star Team Impact Project intake.

The BAASS-MUFON Star Team Impact Project contract itself has never surfaced. MUFON is a private organisation and not FOIA-able, but the contract terms would establish what civilian case data flowed into a federally funded program.

KONA BLUE's proposal package at DHS: AARO characterises it but the underlying documents have been released only in part. DHS FOIA for the O'Toole-era Science and Technology Directorate SAP proposal file is the route.

Whether James Clapper was briefed on any material beyond the DIRD deliverables before recommending against the SAP in November 2009. He has never been asked on the record about the memorandum bearing his recommendation.
